posts.text:
Musings of the Day, 10/11/26

Last night was my 20th Metallica show, and I had the opportunity to sit down with Kirk and Rob at the meet n’ greet beforehand and ask them a question I’ve had forever about the first time I saw them back in summer of 1988 at Monsters of Rock, LA Coliseum.

Metallica played 3rd, after Kingdom Come and Dokken and before Scorpions and Van Halen. I had nosebleeds along with my buddies back in the day, but when Metallica came on, all hell broke loose, and about 20,000 people rushed the stage — including us! I just remember dodging pieces of chair shrapnel and charging forward in the mob and eventually making it up to the very front for the rest of the show, because the security staff gave up and left after the KAOS.

According to Kirk, the pandemonium was accidentally instigated by the band “inviting” everyone to come up and join them up front, forgetting that the massive GA pit area had all these plastic chairs bolted down. Well, the fan mob tore through the whole section, and they had to stop the show and have a “cooling off” period before restarting, because Kirk said that they saw waves of chairs being thrown forward and eventually being thrown on stage and the promoter freaked out! 

Fast forward to the present — last night I almost got kicked out of the Sphere for starting a mosh pit. WTF. What happened to the 80’s???

🤘🤘🤘

posts.name: nunchuk_io
posts.text:
A few words given the recent exploits on hardware signing devices:

• The Ledger supply chain attack represents one of the most sophisticated attacks thus far on the wallet ecosystem. In many ways it’s a lot more sophisticated than the Coldcard RNG exploit, because that one was software only. This one took a cross-border company buyout, tampering with the devices (implanting an eSIM, an LTE module and a CPU) and manufacturing the implants at scale.

• These sorts of attacks have been predicted by early Bitcoiners, but in Bitcoin they remained theoretical or crude until this year. It shows that the level of sophistication of attacks has risen quickly, and what was previously “good enough” advice on wallets and self-custody is no longer sufficient.

• When we started Nunchuk a few years ago, our premise was that multisig, and multi-vendor multisig, needs to become the standard for self-custody in the future. But even we didn’t expect how fast it would materialize. This is likely due to 2 factors: Bitcoin getting more mainstream, and the rise of AI-assisted attacks. This is a Sputnik moment for Bitcoin self-custody. The defenses need to level up.

• Passphrases wouldn’t have helped in the Ledger case, since you are required to enter the passphrase into the device for it to sign any transactions. A compromised device that phones home the seed phrase can also easily phone home the passphrase the moment you enter it.

• Similarly, generating the private key somewhere else (even by rolling dice) and subsequently importing it onto a tampered device wouldn’t save you here. The device can phone home the seed phrase the moment it’s imported.

• Anti-tampering techniques might help, such as transparent casing or bricking the device if it’s tampered with. Or forever displaying a message once the seal is broken. Or using on-device encryption between the internal hardware components. But a dedicated and resourceful enough attacker can still find ways to get around these layers. Tampering and anti-tampering have long been a cat-and-mouse game. In 2008, card readers doctored right off a Chinese production line sent card data and PINs over mobile networks to Pakistan. The Ledger attack is the same playbook, 18 years later. The bigger the target, the more attackers spend on overcoming the defenses.

• You should order directly from the vendors as much as possible, using a PO box for privacy.

• Any setup that relies on a single hardware/software stack or a single vendor should be considered at risk.

• Building your own hardware signers from generic parts is a good option for technical users.

• Multi-vendor multisig should become the standard. Each signer should have a completely independent hardware/software stack from the other signers. The point is that there shouldn’t be any single-point-of-failure anywhere in your setup.

• Many advanced protocols rely on timelocks and the recovery path being a simple singlesig. The recent attacks and exploits should highlight how dangerous this could be. Timelocks simply delay a risk. If a seed is compromised and there’s a timelock involved, the attacker just needs to wait out the timelock. (For Miniscript wallets, there’s the wallet descriptor too, but presumably it also gets sent to the device at some point.) Vault-like protocols face a similar problem: any withdrawal or recovery path that relies on a single key is a potential single point of failure. 

• For our on-chain timelock-assisted wallets, in a few weeks we are adding the option to customize the recovery path to be an M-of-N, so that, if you want, spending would require multiple keys at all points during the wallet’s lifetime.

posts.text:
Something v. strange in the French publishing mafia:
Oliver Nora, head of the publishing house Grasset was making 1.1M Euros in 2025 on 12 M IN TOTAL REVENUE, not counting another 1M expense alloc.

Grasset isn't a startup, but the 2nd most established publisher.

That caste controls French publishing.

quoted.text:
Chez Grasset, Olivier NORA touchait un SALAIRE quasiment équivalent à la part fixe de Bernard ARNAULT chez LVMH !

- Bernard Arnault chez LVMH : 1,138 M€ de part fixe dans sa rémunération annuelle de mandataire social.

- Olivier Nora chez Grasset : 1,017 M€ de salaire annuel, selon Vincent Bolloré.

Sauf que :

LVMH, c’est 84,7 MILLIARDS € de chiffre d’affaires et plus de 215 000 salariés dans le monde. Grasset, c’est 16,48 MILLIONS € de chiffre d’affaires et environ 38 salariés à Paris.

Soit une rémunération presque comparable, dans une société dont le chiffre d’affaires est environ 5 000 fois inférieur.

Rapportée au chiffre d’affaires de Grasset, la rémunération d'Olivier Nora représentait environ 6,2 % du chiffre d'affaires annuel.

À ce ratio, Bernard Arnault ne toucherait pas 1,138 M€ de fixe chez LVMH, mais environ... 5,2 MILLIARDS € !

Et ce n’est pas tout.

Dans les comptes 2024 de Grasset, la ligne « salaires et traitements » atteint 2,32 M€.

Nora pesait donc l’équivalent de 44 % de cette ligne. C’est précisément ce qui explique qu’une partie de sa rémunération ait été, en réalité, prise en charge par la société mère, Hachette.

À titre de comparaison, la rémunération fixe + variable versée de Bernard Arnault représente environ 0,02 % des frais de personnel annuels du groupe LVMH.

Peut-être que Virginie Despentes, grande critique de "l’argent-roi", aura un avis sur cette concentration salariale exceptionnelle ?

@satyanadella extremely well put. I have been saying this, not as elegantly - we cannot rely on the disclosures of frontier LLMs alone:
1. These harnesses need to be constructed so that third parties can get involved in observability and transparency..
2. As we get there we also can imagine users (enterprises) wanting to adapt the guardrails to their values, principles and business practices. One cannot imagine a global set of guardrails owned by the model creators. 
3. No real business will be able to implement the enhanced capabilites of models if they remain black boxes, auditability, verification and compliance are essential premises to ensure that businesses can continue to operate showing duty of care. 
4. Information securty architectures are consistent over decades, the AI architectures need to make room for us to be able to interface seamlessly, at speed and consistently - today all attempts by us are jerry rigged and band aids because we are trying to adapt to the speed of the model providers. If the AI industry doesn't support the simultaneous capability of the security industry things will stall.
5. To foster the diffusion of AI at speed and build trust we need to have momentum behind the conversation just initiated by Satya.
